analysis.one_liner: Requires a five-cent refund deposit on beer and soft drink containers nationwide, with a ban on pull-tab cans.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and died there without a vote or any further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every beer, soda, and similar beverage container sold nationwide to carry a refund value of at least five cents, paid back to anyone returning the empty container to a store or distributor. It would also have banned metal cans with pull-tab openings and let the EPA work out how stores get compensated for handling returns. Its stated aims were cutting litter, reducing the solid waste stream, and shifting disposal costs away from local governments.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who live with litter, pay local taxes for waste disposal, or want refundable containers: the bill put a five-cent refund on beer and soda containers, cutting the waste stream by an estimated 5 to 10 percent per its findings, and banned sharp pull-tab cans that pose hazards to children. Communities near beaches and parks would have seen the most visible cleanup.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities burdened by litter and trash costs

how_it_helps.text: Requires a refund value of at least five cents on beer, soft drink, and similar beverage containers, so people can redeem empties rather than throw them away.

The bill's own findings state that recycling beverage containers would cut the national solid waste stream by an estimated 5 to 10 percent and reduce the disposal cost burden on local and state governments.
Bans metal cans with detachable pull-tab openings, which littering turns into sharp hazards for children and others.

analysis.who_pays: Beverage distributors and retailers, who would have to print refund values, accept and pay refunds on returned containers, and adjust logistics; packaging and container makers, who could sell fewer single-use one-way containers; and, to a small extent, consumers who pay the deposit up front (recovered on return).
analysis.who_pays_short: Beverage distributors, retailers, and container makers

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state and local container-deposit laws to the extent the EPA Administrator finds them inconsistent, which could weaken tougher existing state laws and set a national floor rather than a ceiling.
Retailers would have to take back and pay refunds on returned containers of brands they sell, adding handling work for small stores until any handler's fee is created.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — less litter and less solid waste to bury or burn, lower disposal costs for cities, energy saved through reuse — are real, and similar state bottle bills have proven effective and cheap to run. The costs fall on beverage and packaging companies, who would have to manage a return system, and in a small way on consumers at the point of sale, which the deposit system largely offsets for people who return containers. The bill also included a study of whether retailers should be paid a handling fee, showing some attention to store-level burdens. On balance the costs are modest and borne mostly by industry, while the benefits are broadly shared.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, was never reported out, and died when the 101st Congress ended without ever reaching the floor.

narrative.text: The only action ever taken on the bill was its introduction on May 9, 1989 and its referral that same day to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No vote, markup, or committee report followed, and the Congress ended January 3, 1991 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Beverage and container makers, who avoided the cost of a national deposit-refund system, and state and local governments that continued carrying the disposal burden.

for.name: Mark O. Hatfield
for.what_they_did: Introduced the national bottle bill and sought Senate action on it.

for.name: James Jeffords
for.what_they_did: Joined in introducing the bill at its first Senate reading.

for.name: 6 senators (4 of 55 Democrats, 2 of 45 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it small bipartisan support in the Senate.

against.name: Beverage and container industries
against.role: Soft drink and brewing companies, can and bottle manufacturers, and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Long opposed mandatory deposit legislation, lobbying against national bottle bills as costly and as a threat to the one-way container business.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after referral: no markup, no report, no vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship (a Republican lead sponsor with both Democratic and Republican cosponsors), but it never progressed far enough for a party-line vote to occur.

industries.industry: Beverage and packaging makers (soft drinks, brewers, can and bottle manufacturers)
industries.note: A mandatory deposit system forces them to print refund values, take back containers, and pay refunds, adding handling and reverse-logistics costs. The detachable pull-tab ban also forces packaging changes.

Stores would have to accept and pay refunds on returned containers of brands they sell, adding counter work, though the bill lets the EPA restrict redemption numbers and directs a study of a fee to cover their handling costs.
Less beverage-container trash means lower solid waste disposal costs for cities and towns, a savings the bill's findings explicitly cite.
